candidateRows: Transformative religious experience makes God the most natural explanation of a life-changing personal encounter.
This supplies experiential support for theism and connects lived religious experience directly to the motion's explanatory comparison.
After discussing Ward's philosophical conversion, the host asks whether his Christian commitment also rests on experience rather than intellectual assent alone.
Consciousness remains a profound and perhaps permanently insoluble problem, supporting agnosticism without pointing specifically to Christianity.
This establishes the con side's central stance that naturalism may acknowledge consciousness as mysterious without converting that mystery into theism.
The host's suggestion that consciousness may challenge atheism by requiring a reality beyond the natural world.
Following a documentary segment about the brain's complexity, the host asks whether the human mind has challenged Ruse's atheistic outlook.
Because conscious experience is epistemically immediate while brains are theoretically inferred, eliminative materialism undermines the basis of knowledge.
This is a foundational pro argument against reducing mind to matter and begins Ward's positive route from the primacy of experience toward theism.
The materialist position, associated by the host with Daniel Dennett, that mental life can receive a wholly physical explanation.
After Ruse describes consciousness as unsolved, the host asks Ward why a purely material and naturalistic explanation of mind is inadequate.
The explanatory gap between brain and mind remains unbridged, but ignorance about that gap neither refutes naturalism nor makes invoking God helpful.
The move concedes the hard problem while blocking the pro side's main inference from scientific incompleteness to a God-centered explanation.
Ward's argument that consciousness cannot be scientifically reduced and places inquiry on a path toward something like God.
The host asks Ruse about physicalist accounts from Dennett and the Churchlands after Ward argues that no scientific explanation can bridge consciousness and brain activity.
If consciousness is the fundamental substance of reality, idealism makes the transition to a universal divine consciousness comparatively short.
This states Ward's positive mind-first ontology and makes the central inferential connection from consciousness as fundamental reality to God.
Ruse's contention that the ultimate mystery of why anything exists cannot be solved by Ward's position either.
Ruse agrees that the existence of reality is genuinely mysterious but denies that Ward can solve it; Ward responds by presenting idealism as the relevant metaphysical ground.
A lawful causal connection between neural firing and perception does not establish identity, so thoughts without brains remain philosophically possible.
The argument preserves the conceptual possibility of disembodied mentality, which is necessary for Ward's broader mind-first and theistic account.
The host's proposed inference that neuronal electrical activity produces a perceived image and therefore explains the mental event.
After a documentary clip describes the unresolved transition from neurons to thought, the host challenges Ward with the example of neural activity producing a red-apple image.
Calling reality idealist does not remove the need to distinguish real persons from imagined ones and therefore adds no explanatory value or reason for God.
This challenges whether Ward's preferred ontology performs explanatory work, pressing that ordinary reality and fantasy still require independent discrimination.
Ward's claim that causal separability permits thoughts without brains and supports treating consciousness as metaphysically fundamental.
Ward argues that a brain state causing a perception does not make the two inseparable; the host then asks Ruse whether science instead supports brain-dependent thought.
Material reality is not known to be fundamental; consciousness is more basic, and some mindlike conscious ground is necessary for any universe to exist.
This is Ward's clearest direct formulation of the mind-first case that God, or something relevantly Godlike, grounds the universe rather than being an optional addition.
Ruse's objection that idealism merely complicates the distinction between reality and imagination and gives no reason to introduce God.
Ruse argues that idealism fails to clarify reality and asks why either idealism or God should be introduced; Ward answers by denying that matter is known to be fundamental.
Near-death reports are scientifically implausible, philosophically inconclusive, disconnected from God, and irrelevant to Christianity's bodily resurrection doctrine.
This attacks an offered empirical route to disembodied consciousness and separately denies that such evidence would establish either God or specifically Christian teaching.
The documentary's claim that cognition during complete brain shutdown would demonstrate mind as a separate entity with relevance to the God question.
A documentary segment presents reports of cognition during clinical death as evidence that mind may continue when the brain is inactive, and the host asks Ruse to respond.
Research into mentality without brain activity matters because it treats bodiless consciousness as possible, and God is defined as a bodiless thinking and willing being.
The move links the empirical possibility of brain-independent consciousness to the metaphysical coherence of God while carefully declining to make it central to faith.
Ruse's argument that near-death evidence is dubious science, poor philosophy, and irrelevant to both God and Christianity.
After Ruse rejects near-death reports as implausible and religiously irrelevant, the host asks Ward whether such cases have any importance for his inquiry.
Personal survival should be understood as the same person being embodied with a different body and brain, rather than as a disembodied soul.
The move specifies Ward's account of mind, embodiment, and survival, clarifying how his position differs from straightforward substance dualism.
The moderator's question whether Ward believes an immaterial soul survives the death of the brain.
Following discussion of mental activity without brain activity, Ward explains resurrection as continuity of the person through embodiment in a different physical form.
Conceivability does not establish reasonableness or truth, and reports of near-death experiences provide little reliable support for mind-body dualism.
This directly contests the evidential transition from possible disembodied mentality to a credible dualist or theistic account of consciousness.
Ward's claim that experiments concerning mentality without ordinary brain activity make bodiless mind thinkable.
Ruse allows that dualism may be logically possible while arguing that near-death reports are vulnerable to projection and do not make the hypothesis reasonable.
God should be conceived as the conscious, purposive, intelligent ground of the universe rather than as an external agent who periodically interferes with it.
The move supplies the core mind-first conception of God that connects consciousness and purpose to the ultimate character of reality.
Ruse's accusation that Ward slides from naturalistic possibility toward recommending belief in God.
After Ruse objects that Ward turns possibility into belief, Ward reframes theism as a claim about the universe's intelligent mental ground.
Religious belief is rooted in putative experience of revelation and nonphysical mind, while philosophy tests whether that experiential interpretation is coherent.
This identifies Ward's principal epistemic route to theism and explains the supporting rather than foundational role assigned to philosophical argument.
Ruse's charge that Ward imports an elaborate theological ontology without showing that it helps explain consciousness.
Ward answers that he begins with revelation and experience of God, then asks whether nonsensory awareness of another mental being is possible and coherent.
Religious experiences can be explained through evolved agency detection and imagination, while their cultural diversity and lack of repeatability weaken their evidential force.
The move offers the principal naturalistic account of religious experience and a direct reason not to infer a transcendent object from such experiences.
Ward's claim that religious faith may be grounded in genuine nonsensory experience of a nonphysical divine mind.
Ruse attributes religious perception to adaptive sensitivities combined with imagination and stresses that conflicting traditions lack science's repeatable universality.
Cross-cultural religious experiences may share a common experiential core despite differing interpretations, and evolutionary persistence may count in favor of their truth.
This counters the naturalistic debunking argument by separating shared experience from variable interpretation and turning evolutionary survival toward reliability.
Ruse's evolutionary explanation of religion and his appeal to incompatible traditions as evidence against religious experience.
Ward argues that diverse theological concepts can interpret a common sense of transcendent loving power and asks whether adaptive survival supports truth-tracking.
God is unnecessary for morality because moral obligation is an evolution-produced social illusion rather than an independently grounded ultimate reality.
The move extends agnostic naturalism from consciousness and religion to moral experience, denying that morality supplies an independent route to theism.
Ward's suggestion that pragmatic and moral usefulness may support adopting a belief and potentially connect morality with God.
Ruse interprets Ward as linking moral and social experience to a creative ground, then rejects that inference by treating morality as genetically generated.
The experienced authority of obligations that bind regardless of desire supports taking morality as real and creates a significant connection between morality and God.
This provides Ward's positive moral-experience argument against evolutionary debunking and links objective obligation to the broader God-centered account.
Ruse's contention that morality is an evolutionary illusion with no ultimate justification and therefore requires no God.
Ward appeals to widespread awareness of duties that override preference, arguing that serious acceptance of such duties resists Ruse's skeptical reduction.
Meaningful human freedom is compatible with causal determination, so affirming free will does not require libertarian agency or an appeal to God.
The move gives agnostic naturalism a direct account of agency, addressing whether a physical causal order can accommodate freedom without theism.
The moderator's challenge that a purely physical brain may reduce apparent control and free will to deterministic autopilot.
Ruse distinguishes libertarianism from compatibilism, notes that Christians also divide on the issue, and endorses causally determined but worthwhile freedom.
The deepest question about freedom is whether the universe arose by blind necessity or through thought and intention, in which case creation itself was free.
The move connects agency to the debate's ultimate contrast between an unintended natural order and a mind-first reality grounded in purposive creation.
Ruse's compatibilist claim that causal determinism permits meaningful freedom without requiring God or libertarian agency.
Ward accepts that Christians differ about human free will but shifts attention to whether reality originates necessarily or through knowledgeable, uncoerced intention.
Shared wonder at existence, natural regularities, consciousness, morality, and freedom does not uniquely support theism because the same experiences admit radically different interpretations.
This concluding synthesis directly addresses whether the phenomena under debate make best sense within theism or remain compatible with an agnostic naturalistic interpretation.
Keith Ward's appeal to the unexplained existence of natural regularities and related mysteries as congenial to a God-centered account.

After Ward expresses amazement at regularities in nature, Ruse agrees that existence and laws are mysterious but argues that they interpret the same experiences through fundamentally different paradigms.
